transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, they brought me in. My family, I mean. They got all worked up about what happened down at the county fair. I was supposed to be giving my talk, and I ended up climbing right up onto this big tractor they had on display. Which, let me tell you, those new models are nothing but plastic and computers. Back in '85, my dad bought this Massey Ferguson, red as a barn door, and that thing ran for thirty years without a single electrical issue. You just can't trust the microchips they put in everything now. They even put them in the cows' ears, did you know that? Beeping all over the pasture, tracking them from space. 

Anyway, I was up in the cab of that display tractor, and I kept jerking the controls around because I needed to show the crowd the new pattern. The new pattern for the fields, you know? It's very important for the soil. If you don't rotate the crops at the right angles, the dirt just turns to dust, like back in the 30s. My grandfather lived through the Dust Bowl, used to tell me how the sky turned black at noon. He kept his teeth in a jar by the sink. But the crowd at the fair, they just didn't understand the pattern. People started yelling at me to get down, waving their hands and hollering, but I couldn't make myself stop moving the levers. I just couldn't stop, I had to finish showing them how the pattern worked. So... they pulled me down and made me come here.
How much sleep have you been getting over the past few days?

Sleep? Well, I haven't really needed much of that lately. Most nights I just sit back in my chair... maybe I get two or three hours of shut-eye, or sometimes none at all. It's a good chair, though. Got it over at Miller's Hardware before the old man died and his son took over the business. That boy doesn't know a thing about good furniture, tried to sell me a leather sofa. You can't have leather in a farmhouse, not with the dogs coming in and out. Old Buster, my hound, he'd scratch that right to pieces. 

But anyway, I'll just be in that chair and then I'm up way before the sun, feeling completely charged. Just ready to work the place like nothing happened. And it's beautiful out there before dawn, you know? Just me and the coyotes down by the creek. You ever hear a pack of coyotes get going in the dark? Sounds like a bunch of teenagers laughing, or sometimes like a woman screaming. Sends a chill right through you if you aren't used to it. But I don't mind, I've got to get out there with my flashlight and check the perimeter wire anyway because the deer keep pushing through the bottom strand, and if you don't keep that tension tight, the whole fence line sags.

Depressed? Well, I don't know about that. I mean, sure, sometimes things get a little slow around the farm, especially in the winter. You ever try breaking ice in the water troughs when it's ten below? The axe just bounces right off, and your hands get so cold you can't even feel the handle. That's when you really miss having a good pair of insulated gloves. I had a pair once, leather with sheep's wool lining, bought them at a farm supply store over in the next county. Best gloves I ever owned, until my dog Buster got hold of them. He chewed the thumb right off the left one. I tried to patch it with some duct tape, but it just wasn't the same. Duct tape is great for a lot of things, you know? Like fixing a cracked taillight or holding a broken shovel handle together, but it's no good for gloves. It just gets stiff in the cold and cracks right off. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being depressed. I don't know, I just keep busy, you know? There's always something to fix or clean or build. You can't just sit around feeling sorry for yourself when there's work to be done.
Have you ever had another time in your life before this where you felt this energized and went days with barely any sleep?

Well, sure, I've had times like this before. If I think about it, over the past year or so, these stretches where I'm just completely charged up and don't need to sleep... they've probably taken up about ten months out of the year. It's just how it goes sometimes. You get on a roll and you just can't stop. Like when we had to replace the roof on the main barn back in '98. A storm came through and took half the shingles right off. Just ripped them up like paper. I was up there for three days straight, hammering away. I had this old Estwing hammer, solid steel handle with a leather grip. They don't make them like that anymore. Now it's all fiberglass and rubber, and the balance is just all wrong. You try swinging one of those new hammers all day, and your elbow will be screaming by supper time. But that Estwing, it was like an extension of my arm. I could drive a ten-penny nail with two swings, bam, bam, done. I dropped it in the tall grass out by the silo a few years back and never could find it. I even took the metal detector out there, the one I bought at a garage sale from old Mrs. Higgins. She was selling all her husband's things after he passed. He had quite a collection of antique fishing lures, too. Some of those wooden ones with the glass eyes, they go for good money now. But anyway, yeah, about ten months out of the past year or so, I've just been going and going like that.
Do you ever hear voices, sounds, or see things that other people who are around don't seem to hear or see?

Voices? Yeah, I do hear things sometimes. Mostly out by the north pasture, especially when it's getting close to dusk. I'll be out there checking the irrigation lines, and I'll hear these clear voices coming right out of the pipes. They tell me which rows are poisoned and which ones are blessed. And the funny thing is, they talk to me even during those weeks when I'm not all fired up and energetic, just regular weeks. 

Speaking of irrigation, you know, those old aluminum pipes are getting harder and harder to find parts for. The new PVC stuff is alright, I guess, but it gets brittle in the sun. I had a joint crack on me last summer, right in the middle of a dry spell. Water spraying everywhere, washing out a whole row of sweet corn. I had to wade in there in my rubber boots—the green ones, you know, with the steel toe. Bought those at a farm auction about five years ago. The fella selling them had feet two sizes bigger than mine, so I have to wear three pairs of wool socks just to keep them from slipping off. Good wool socks, though. My sister knits them for me every Christmas. She uses this yarn she gets from a lady down in Texas who raises alpacas. Alpacas are strange-looking creatures, don't you think? Like a llama but with a worse haircut. I thought about getting a couple once to guard the sheep, but Buster would probably just chase them all over the county. He chased a skunk under the porch once, and man, the smell didn't leave for a month. We had to wash him in tomato juice three times. But anyway, yeah, the voices in the pipes, they tell me about the rows.

Well, let's see... how long? I'd say there were several quieter weeks, you know, times when I wasn't feeling all fired up or grand or anything. Just regular days. But I still heard the lines talking to me, clear as day. And I still knew the farm data was carrying those hidden warnings about the crops. 

Speaking of data, you wouldn't believe the kind of computer systems they try to sell you for farming these days. GPS this, satellite tracking that. I had a fella from the co-op come out in a shiny white pickup truck—didn't even have a speck of mud on the tires, which tells you something right there. He wanted me to buy this tablet thing that mounts right on the tractor dashboard. Said it would tell me exactly how much fertilizer to put down per square foot. I told him my grandfather farmed this land with a mule and a good sense of smell, and he did just fine. That mule, old Barnaby, he lived to be almost thirty. Toughest animal I ever saw. He got out once and ate half of Mrs. Gable's prize-winning petunias. She was so mad she threatened to call the sheriff, but I brought her a basket of fresh peaches from the orchard and that smoothed things over. Peaches were real good that year, sweet and juicy. You just don't get peaches like that from the supermarket. They pick them green and gas them to turn color, you know. It's a crying shame. But anyway, yeah, even on those quieter weeks, the warnings and the voices were still there.
